# Student data, copyright and institutional policy

Your own teaching material is yours to use with these tools; student work and third-party material are not. Most of the risk in using an agent for teaching comes from the second and third categories, and your university sets the rules for both. This chapter is general guidance and not legal advice.

**Three kinds of material.**

| Material | Examples | Default position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your own | Your notes, slides, questions, code | Free to use, subject to your employer's IP policy |
| Student | Scripts, coursework, marks, emails, extenuating circumstances | Approved tools only, anonymised, and often not at all |
| Third party | Textbook chapters, publisher slides and test banks, journal articles, licensed datasets | Depends on the licence; ask the library |

**Student data.** A script with a name or student number on it is personal data, and your university is responsible for how it is processed. Published UK policies are consistent on the default:

- [Liverpool](https://www.liverpool.ac.uk/about/the-university/reports-policies-and-governance/ai-at-liverpool/policies-and-guidance/guidance-learning-teaching-and-assessment) lists uploading student work or personal data to public AI platforms as unacceptable without a data protection impact assessment or advice from the Data Protection Officer.
- [York](https://www.york.ac.uk/about/ai/education/marking_and_feedback/) requires explicit student permission before student work or details go into a generative AI tool.
- [Exeter](https://www.exeter.ac.uk/v8media/specificsites/epqs/Guidance_on_AI_in_Marking_and_Feedback.pdf) notes that student work is by default the student's intellectual property.

Anonymising helps but does not settle the matter: an essay can identify its author through its content, and the work still belongs to the student.

**Approved tools and account types.** Universities approve specific tools under specific contracts. A personal subscription to the same product is a different legal arrangement. The distinction that usually matters is whether the provider may train on what you send and how long it is kept.

> **In Claude Code.** The [data usage page](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage) distinguishes two cases. On personal plans (Free, Pro, Max, Ultra), data is used to train models when the account's setting allows it, with retention of five years if allowed and 30 days if not. Under commercial terms (Team, Enterprise, API), prompts and code are not used for training unless the customer opts in, and standard retention is 30 days.
>
> Session transcripts are also stored on your own machine, unencrypted, for 30 days by default, and transcripts of sessions started in the desktop app are kept with no age limit unless you set one. On a shared or unencrypted laptop, that is a further copy of anything you worked on.

**Connectors.** A connector links the agent to another program or service, such as a cloud drive, a data provider or a statistical package (chapter 5). Anything the agent reads or sends through a connector falls under the same rules as the rest of this chapter, and a connector to an external service is one more place where student work or licensed data can end up. Before using a connector in a folder that holds student work or licensed material, check what it reads and sends, and to whom. Your university's approval of the agent may not cover the services its connectors reach.

> **In Claude Code.** Connectors are [MCP servers](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp). The documentation advises verifying that you trust each server before connecting it, because a server that fetches external content can expose the agent to prompt injection: instructions hidden in that content which the agent may follow. Even a connector that runs on your own computer, such as the MATLAB server, may send usage data to its developer.

**Third-party teaching material.** Putting a textbook chapter or a publisher's test bank into a prompt is likely to count as copying for copyright purposes. Whether it is licensed depends on your university's agreements.

- The Copyright Licensing Agency added permission for copying into generative AI prompts to its business licences in May 2025. For the Higher Education licence, publishers were [consulted in summer 2026](https://www.alpsp.org/news-publications/industry-news/pls-consultation-on-workplace-generative-ai-permissions-in-cla-education-and-higher-education-licences/) on adding equivalent permissions. Whether these are now in force was not confirmed at the time of writing, so ask your library.
- Where such permissions exist in other CLA licences, they exclude training and require a tool whose terms do not allow training on prompts. A personal account with training switched on would not qualify.
- Licensed datasets used in teaching have their own terms. Check before placing them in a folder the agent reads.

**Output that reproduces a source.** An exercise that closely follows a textbook problem may still infringe the publisher's copyright, however it was produced. Ask the agent to write new questions to your specification, and do not ask it to rephrase existing ones.

**Practical rules.**

- Keep student work out of the module folder unless you are using an approved tool for an approved purpose.
- Keep third-party material in a separate subfolder of `sources/` so it is easy to exclude.
- Find your university's list of approved AI tools and its staff guidance before the first use, and reread it each year.
- If the guidance is silent on what you want to do, ask your Director of Education or the data protection team, and keep the answer.
